item.text: {"text":"Recent research supports evaluating evidence grounding separately from explanation plausibility. A [2025 survey of 64 studies](https://aclanthology.org/2025.inlg-main.4/) found inconsistent hallucination definitions and frequent omissions of annotation guidelines and agreement measures. [Mirage (2025)](https://aclanthology.org/2025.findings-emnlp.1035/) found automated hallucination metrics often misaligned with human judgments across datasets and models. These findings support explicit annotation rules and local validation of text proxies; semantic similarity alone cannot establish compatibility, redundancy, or user intent.\n\nFor this task, a proposed taxonomy is: explicit compatibility conflict, requiring documented contradictory specifications; functional redundancy, requiring evidence of overlapping functions while leaving undesirability unjudged unless feedback establishes it; broad association, where shared topic or wording provides only weak relevance evidence; and insufficient information, where available records cannot resolve the claim. Attach exact title/description spans, history identifiers, timestamps, or recorded feedback to every judgment. On the twenty training-user lists, use two independent annotators, preserve initial labels, report raw agreement plus Cohen’s κ or Krippendorff’s α, and adjudicate disagreements. Validate automated proxies against these annotations with per-label precision/recall and confusion counts. [Trust or Escalate (ICLR 2025)](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/08dabd5345b37fffcbe335bd578b15a0-Paper-Conference.pdf) supports selective evaluation: accept sufficiently reliable judgments and abstain otherwise. Report error versus coverage and evaluate thresholds on users excluded from calibration; twenty users support exploratory calibration, not strong generalization claims. Do not infer latent intent, simulator traits, or unavailable reviews and attributes."}
